blocks.text: A Nigerian diplomat in New York sits in the General Assembly. Another in Addis Ababa sits in the African Union. A third walks into the ECOWAS Commission in Abuja. Three halls, three sets of initials — UN, AU, ECOWAS — and one recurring exam question: what is each body for, who runs it, and what has Nigeria done inside it?

blocks.title: International organisation
blocks.text: A standing association of states (and sometimes other actors), created by treaty, with organs and rules of its own, to pursue shared purposes such as peace, trade or regional integration. The United Nations, the African Union and ECOWAS are the three that WAEC, NECO and JAMB test most often.

blocks.markdown:
### The United Nations

The UN was founded in **1945** at San Francisco, succeeding the League of Nations. Nigeria joined on **7 October 1960**, a week after independence.

**Aims** (from the Charter): to maintain international peace and security; to develop friendly relations among nations; to achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems; and to be a centre for harmonising the actions of states.

**Principal organs:**
- **General Assembly** — all member states, one vote each; debates and passes resolutions; elects members of other organs; cannot by itself make binding law in the way the Security Council can on peace and security.
- **Security Council** — 15 members: five permanent (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States) with a **veto**, and ten non-permanent elected for two-year terms. Primary responsibility for peace and security; can impose sanctions and authorise force.
- **Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC)** — coordinates economic, social and specialised-agency work.
- **International Court of Justice (ICJ)** — sits at The Hague; settles legal disputes between states that accept its jurisdiction; Nigeria has used it (notably the Bakassi case with Cameroon).
- **Secretariat** — the international civil service, headed by the Secretary-General.
- **Trusteeship Council** — set up to supervise trust territories; its work is complete and it is inactive.

### From OAU to AU

The **Organisation of African Unity (OAU)** was founded on **25 May 1963** in **Addis Ababa** by 32 independent African states. Its aims were continental unity, the defence of sovereignty, the eradication of colonialism, and non-interference in members' internal affairs. That last principle later looked like a shield for dictators.

The **African Union (AU)** was launched on **9 July 2002** in **Durban**, South Africa, after the Constitutive Act (Lomé, 2000) and the Sirte Declaration (1999). It succeeded the OAU.

**AU objectives** go further than the OAU's: accelerate political and economic integration; promote peace, security and stability; promote democratic principles, human rights and good governance; promote sustainable development; and, crucially, allow **intervention in a member state** in respect of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity — a break with the OAU's rigid non-interference. Organs include the Assembly of Heads of State, the Executive Council, the Permanent Representatives Committee, the AU Commission (Addis Ababa), the Pan-African Parliament, and the Peace and Security Council.

blocks.caption: The three organisations compared. Remember OAU 1963 → AU 2002, ECOWAS 1975 Lagos

items: **Economic integration** — a common market, later a customs union and, in ambition, a single currency; removal of barriers to trade among members.
**Free movement of persons, goods, services and capital** — the protocol on free movement is the citizen-facing achievement, even though implementation is uneven at land borders.
**Cooperation in industry, energy, transport and telecommunications** so that small West African economies can specialise.
**Peace and security** — the 1993 revised treaty and later protocols created a framework for conflict prevention and for ECOMOG-type missions.
**Raising living standards** and strengthening relations among member states.

blocks.title: Nigeria in ECOWAS
blocks.text: Nigeria initiated and hosted the 1975 Lagos treaty, provides a large share of the Community levy, hosts the ECOWAS Commission in Abuja, and supplied most of the troops and money for ECOMOG in Liberia and Sierra Leone. That leadership is the standard 'Nigeria's role' answer — with a note of criticism that neighbours sometimes fear Nigerian dominance.

blocks.title: Tracing OAU to AU and placing ECOWAS beside both
blocks.prompt: A question asks you to distinguish the OAU from the AU and to state Nigeria's role in ECOWAS. Plan a three-part answer.

steps.text: OAU, 25 May 1963, Addis Ababa: unity, sovereignty, end of colonialism, non-interference. Success against colonial and white-minority regimes; weakness against internal dictatorships and economic integration.

AU, launched 9 July 2002, Durban: keeps unity but adds democracy, human rights, economic integration and a right of intervention against genocide and war crimes. Institutions (Commission, Peace and Security Council, Pan-African Parliament) are stronger on paper than the OAU's.
ECOWAS is regional, not continental: 1975 Lagos, revised 1993 Abuja. Aims are West African integration and free movement, plus peacekeeping. Nigeria's role: founder, host, financier, ECOMOG lead.
Keep the scales distinct. UN is global; AU is continental; ECOWAS is West African. A candidate who writes that ECOWAS replaced the OAU has mixed the scales.

blocks.answer: OAU 1963 (non-interference, decolonisation) was succeeded by AU 2002 (integration, democracy, possible intervention). ECOWAS 1975 is the West African economic and security community; Nigeria founded, hosts and has led its peacekeeping

blocks.title: Organs of the UN — six, not three
blocks.text: List all six principal organs: General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, ICJ, Secretariat, Trusteeship Council. Naming only the Assembly and the Council looks like incomplete knowledge. For the Security Council, the veto of the five permanent members is the fact JAMB always wants. Dates: UN 1945, Nigeria joins 1960; OAU 1963; ECOWAS 1975; AU 2002.

points: The UN (1945) aims to keep peace, develop friendly relations, promote cooperation and harmonise states' actions. Nigeria joined on 7 October 1960.
Its six principal organs are the General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, ICJ, Secretariat and Trusteeship Council.
The OAU was founded on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa; the AU succeeded it on 9 July 2002 in Durban, with stronger aims on democracy, integration and intervention against mass atrocities.
ECOWAS was founded by the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975 to integrate West African economies, allow free movement and, later, keep regional peace.
Nigeria is a founding OAU member, host and leading financier of ECOWAS, and the principal contributor to ECOMOG.
